question: Can learnable, nonuniform spline knots and shared activation parameters make B-spline Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks more stable and parameter-efficient than fixed-grid KANs while retaining their function-approximation advantage?

key_findings.claim: The paper bounds the number of one-dimensional spline knots generated by fixed-grid multilayer KANs in terms of grid size, spline order, and depth rather than layer width.
key_findings.evidence: A single fixed-grid layer has G+K shared knots. Theorem 4.3 gives a lower bound G+K and a multiplicative depth-dependent upper bound, with new knots arising only when a previous-layer output spans at least one grid interval. The appendix constructs a sawtooth case intended to show tightness.

anchors.section: 4 Upper Bound of Knots for KAN

key_findings.claim: FR-KAN reduces parameter growth by grouping neurons and sharing linear weights, then recovers activation diversity through trainable grid shifts.
key_findings.evidence: Original per-edge spline coefficients scale as O(d_in d_out (G+K+1)); grouping and shared weights reduce the stated count to O(d_in d_out+h(G+K)). Each group adds learned offsets to a common grid, sorts the shifted coordinates to preserve knot order, and thereby increases the possible unique-knot count to a bound proportional to h.

key_findings.claim: Smoothness regularization and a wider spline domain address the NaN-producing oscillation observed with dense fixed knots.
key_findings.evidence: The method penalizes second derivatives of spline coefficients/activations and expands the default grid range toward [-10,10]. On the STL10 diagnostic, both KAN variants with range [-1,1] terminate with NaN loss, while ranges from [-3,3] onward converge more reliably and FR-KAN is visually smoother on the Feynman I.6.2 example.

key_findings.claim: Across the reported parameter-controlled tasks, FR-KAN usually beats original KAN and often MLP, with its clearest gains on spline-friendly function approximation.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports best image accuracies of about 58% CIFAR-10, 30% CIFAR-100, and 48% STL10; controlled-width Table 1 generally favors FR-KAN. On 14 displayed Feynman equations it has the lowest RMSE in most rows, including 0.9442 versus 1.1485 for KAN on I.6.2 and 0.0407 versus 0.0911 on I.50.26.

method.core_idea: View KAN expressivity and instability through spline-knot placement, share most spline parameters for scale, and learn small ordered grid shifts plus smoothness controls to regain adaptive resolution.
method.mechanism: FR-KAN groups neurons that share basis coefficients, shares the spline and SiLU combination weight, learns per-group offsets to a base grid followed by sorting, penalizes second-derivative variation, and uses a wider grid range. The paper derives fixed- and free-grid knot-count bounds and evaluates parameter-matched networks across vision, text, time series, multimodal, and Feynman-function tasks.
assumptions: One-dimensional knot count is a useful proxy for expressivity of multivariate layered KANs.
Sorting shifted grid points is differentiable enough in practice for gradient training.
Parameter matching provides a fair architectural comparison despite different per-step compute and optimizer behavior.
The selected small benchmarks reflect KAN suitability beyond scientific regression.

techniques.role: Relates fixed-grid KAN expressivity to grid size, degree, and depth.
Amortizes spline coefficients across edges to reduce parameters.
Learns shifted nonuniform knots and sorts them to preserve a valid B-spline grid.
Suppresses high-curvature oscillations and volatile gradients.
Reduces knot crowding and out-of-range activation failures.

evaluations.setting: Parameter-controlled CIFAR-10/100, STL10, and MNIST models
evaluations.result: FR-KAN generally matches or exceeds MLP and KAN; reported best values include 58%, 30%, and 48% on the three harder image datasets.
evaluations.baseline: ReLU MLP, original KAN, Rational-KAN, and RBF-KAN

evaluations.setting: AG News, AVMNIST, MIMIC-III, and ETTh1
evaluations.metric: Task performance at comparable trainable-parameter counts
evaluations.result: FR-KAN is reported as generally strongest and less variable, with MIMIC-III showing substantial noise and variance.
evaluations.baseline: MLP and several KAN basis variants

evaluations.setting: Selected AI Feynman equations, grid size 20
evaluations.result: FR-KAN has the lowest displayed RMSE in most equations, though KAN/RBF/Rational variants win individual rows.
evaluations.baseline: MLP, original KAN, Fourier-KAN, Rational-KAN, and RBF-KAN

evaluations.result: [-1,1] runs fail with NaNs; expanded ranges converge, with FR-KAN visually more stable.
evaluations.baseline: Fixed-grid KAN under the same ranges

limitations: The knot analysis is presented for one-dimensional spline compositions and does not fully characterize multivariate function complexity or generalization.
Several theorem statements and notation are difficult to audit, and the claimed C2-continuity mechanism is described as a penalty rather than an exact constraint.
Only three runs are reported, and many architecture/hyperparameter choices differ across families despite parameter matching.
Wall-clock time, memory, FLOPs, and backward-pass cost are not benchmarked even though recursive B-spline computation is acknowledged as the main drawback.
Benchmarks are relatively small; no large modern backbone establishes scaling.
NaN/Inf-generating Feynman functions are omitted, which may bias the approximation comparison.
failure_modes: Sorted knot offsets cross or cluster, creating nonsmooth optimization and near-singular spline intervals.
Second-derivative penalties oversmooth sharp but genuine target structure.
Wide grid ranges waste resolution where data are concentrated and trade stability for underfitting.
Grouped splines collapse diverse features into too few shared univariate functions.
Parameter parity conceals much higher latency and memory traffic than an MLP.
reusable_insights: Analyze adaptive-basis networks in terms of both basis count and placement, not parameter count alone.
Separate a high-cost expressive basis from cheap edge-specific mixing so the basis can be shared.
Track knot spacing and curvature as explicit training-health metrics.
Report stability as failure frequency and wall-clock efficiency, not only mean accuracy.
Use target-aware nonuniform resolution instead of increasing a uniform grid globally.
open_questions: Can monotone knot parameterizations replace sorting and guarantee minimum spacing?
What finite-sample or approximation-error bound follows from the proposed knot-count result?
Does FR-KAN remain competitive at ResNet, Transformer, or operator-learning scale after equalizing FLOPs?
Which tasks actually benefit from adaptive spline edges rather than conventional MLP features?
Can fused linear-time kernels remove the recursive backward-graph overhead?

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: The original KAN assigns learned B-spline functions to edges and emphasizes scientific interpretability; FR-KAN targets its fixed-grid, parameter, and stability costs with sharing and movable knots.

competitive_landscape.title: MatrixKAN: Parallelized Kolmogorov-Arnold Network
competitive_landscape.difference: MatrixKAN retains B-splines but rewrites recursive evaluation as parallel matrix operations and reports roughly 40x speedups; FR-KAN reduces trainable parameters and adjusts knots but leaves kernel-level recursion overhead open.

competitive_landscape.title: Free-RBF-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Adaptive Radial Basis Functions for Efficient Function Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Free-RBF-KAN also learns adaptive centers and smoothness but uses nonrecursive radial bases with a universality proof and structured scientific tasks; it directly attacks the runtime limitation FR-KAN acknowledges.

competitive_landscape.title: LTBs-KAN: Linear-Time B-splines Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: LTBs-KAN derives linear-time base-spline evaluation and factorizes parameters, prioritizing measured computation; FR-KAN's distinctive element is adaptive ordered knots plus a knot-count analysis.

novelty_assessment: Learning ordered knot shifts while grouping spline parameters is a sensible KAN-specific combination, and the paper usefully centers stability on knot crowding and curvature. Theoretical and empirical claims are less mature than the architectural intuition: the knot-count proxy is narrow, exact smoothness guarantees are unclear, and later basis/evaluation methods more directly address runtime.
